items.title: I Made a React App
items.summary: I made a React App. Well, I'm not quite done yet. There's some stuff I'd like to work out, such as useContext, and extracting my useEffect logic from the App component and into their own functions. But the app is working - I rebuilt an app I had already made using vanilla JavaScript. The two apps are functionally identical, but I thought it might be worth noting the differences somewhere.
items.content_html:
I made a React App. Well, I'm not quite done yet. There's some stuff I'd like to work out, such as useContext, and extracting my useEffect logic from the App component and into their own functions. But the app is working - I rebuilt an app I had already made using vanilla JavaScript. The two apps are functionally identical, but I thought it might be worth noting the differences somewhere.

The pros and cons of React have been heavily documented for years, so don't expect to read anything groundbreaking here. This is merely a reflection on some learning I've done lately.

I try to avoid unnecessary JavaScript where I can. I think HTML should be able to most things in a static site, JavaScript enhancements should ideally be modular and complimentary. In the situation where you don't have access to, or don't need a back-end server for something more functional, then I guess JavaScript is allowed.

A while ago I threw together a "web app" of sorts, that was intended as a complimentary tool for a project that piped scheduled TV shows that I follow to a Google Calendar. The web page existed only as a quick way to find show ID's without having to go through a bloated and over-informative front-end. It just showed me what I needed, nothing else. Oh, I did throw episodes by season in there as an excuse to play around with Simple CSS.

The app worked as intended. It wasn't fancy. It had terrible accessibility. But it did what I wanted it to. It connected to an API and updated the DOM accordingly. I made some design choices that were intended to reduce API calls out of respect to TV Maze, and keeping the calls to a minimum. I haven't gone back to fix the accessibility yet - as I've had it on the back of my mind that I would like to revisit the project, and skip the Google Apps Script phase and just print the schedule directly into an iCal file. I've been learning about iCal and I'm about ready to start that when my daily schedule allows.

I caught wind of something called web components in that time. They sound interesting. The kind of functionality you would get from a front-end framework, but natively in the browser. I've decided that might be something I might like to implement when I eventually go back to the project and inevitably get round to cleaning up the web page.

I've only ever really coded JavaScript in a JQuery without JQuery fashion. That is: I chop up and change the DOM based on events. At most I'll wrap the code in an App Class Object if the script is critical to the website. But nothing fancy like React. I looked at it years ago, I didn't really get on board. I wasn't making anything big, and the docs were a bit of mess during the transition from class based to function components.

I've learned a bit of it now. While I was reading about web components, it dawned on me that I don't really understand how a framework should work. It might be overkill, but I learned React, and will look at Lit components too, to work backwards to native web components.

I enjoyed the React development process. Though I still think it isn't really necessary for the size of projects I tend to work on - I can see why a large project with many devs would stand to benefit from the process. It is nice to work on things modularly, and in somewhat isolation from the rest of the code base - that's a concept I can get on board with, and I might actually be starting to look forward to using web components, even if I don't use them often.

What I didn't enjoy about using React is NodeJS is that it simply moves too fast. Trying to deploy my app on my Coolify instance was a headache. Using vite@latest just wouldn't work for me. I was getting BadEngine errors in my Docker container and then the deployment process would throw an error and exit. It deployed to Netlify with no issues at all, but I would expect this one as Netlify's main purposes for existing is to do exactly that. I eventually got a working Coolify deployment using vite@7, although even having to do that in the first place made me very aware that NodeJS will quickly change and vite version 7.x will no longer be supported and I'd likely have to go through the headache of updating everything. Curiously, I still got the same BadEngine errors, but the deployment completed this time, and everything is apparently okay now that I've set up health checks on the deployment (shrugs).

The old vanilla app is functionally identical to the new React app, with a static asset or two missing or different depending on when you look at it. The React app is running on a Pi at time of writing, so uptime and availability may vary. The expected differences apply: my ~5kB JavaScript file has been replaced with a ~200kB index-hash.js file, and the total size difference has jumped from ~45kB to ~237kB. If I'm being completely honest, I thought the React app size was going to be much bigger than that - maybe they've trimmed off some fat in the last few years? If that's the case, then well done to those responsible.

Memory usage is higher for the React app in firefox by almost double, from ~2MB compared to ~4MB, though React seems to manage memory over time better than the vanilla JS app. And memory usage for both apps seems to go between ~40MB and ~45MB for both apps in Chromium.

Performance differs a lot less than I had anticipated between React and JS. Although I still pride myself on keeping things small when they don't need to be big, so I won't be switching soon. But the process as a whole has made me keen to see how things stack up with the Lit library as well as native web components.

items.title: An Amateurs Take on NextCloud
items.summary: I've been using NextCloud on a VPS running Ubuntu for perhaps a year now. I didn't have any server experience prior to setting it up. It was a little scary at first, but it's been a learning journey that, overall, I think I've enjoyed so far.
items.content_html:
I've been using NextCloud on a VPS running Ubuntu for perhaps a year now. I didn't have any server experience prior to setting it up. It was a little scary at first, but it's been a learning journey that, overall, I think I've enjoyed so far.

I am by no means an expert yet. But I have conquered the inertia that is caused by the thought: "it might be too difficult for me". Since setting it up I have also gained the courage to convert an old Raspberry Pi into a Coolify server at home.

At this point it is worth noting that I've already written a piece about NextCloud, but that was just a short tech review, and while I may repeat some points here, I intend to look a little deeper at my experience of setting up and running my own NextCloud instance over the past year.

Setting up the NextCloud server in the first place was the hardest bit. Things may have changed since when I first used it, but Hostinger's All-In-One NextCloud image installs either a Docker or a Snap image - I can't actually remember which one anymore. But I do remember that it meant the NextCloud documentation didn't exactly line up well with user experience - as it assumes you are working with a LAMP installation. As a first-timer, I couldn't figure out how to set up the DNS. Having learned a little more about running Linux servers, it might be interesting to see if I could figure that out now or not after a little levelling up - but currently there's no real need, everything is working - if it's not broken, don't fix it. In the end the easy option, while it sets you up with a fully working NextCloud server within a few minutes, turned out not to be the easiest when it came time to configure DNS, adjust the config.php file and run occ tasks.

I had previously subscribed to a NextCloud provider. The providers get to choose what apps are installed on their respective instances. So switching to self hosted, I got total control over what apps I had running on my instance. My VPS is only 1 vCPU core, so while OnlyOffice ran, I couldn't quite get the sync right between server and local files - which appears to be a known bug. NextCloud Office, based on Collabora requires a second vCPU to run well, so I didn't really bother with that one after immediately encountering considerable lag. An online office suite has become less important to me since my employer has developed some kind of fetish of using check boxes in Word Documents, which work in LibreOffice and not in OnlyOffice one day, then in OnlyOffice but not LibreOffice another day. Eventually I got fed up with switching editors and just began using my employers OneDrive and Word suites in a Chromium browser for anything to do with work, and I use locally installed LibreOffice synced to my NextCloud for anything personal.

Other apps I've used include Recipe's and News, both of which sync directly into the SQL database instead of a directory. This requires Redis to be installed and configured, and a Cron job instead of AJAX. I had issues with a major update recently and couldn't see much evidence of other users having similar issues. I'm still learning how to read Logs, but it appeared to be failing at the back up phase, and I think either the apps or my redis config may have been causing the issue here.

Thankfully, NextCloud's desktop client creates synchronised local backups on whatever device you have it installed on, so when I couldn't solve the issue, I simply logged out of my instance on my local devices, made a copy of the NextCloud folder, and installed the new NextCloud version onto a clean Ubuntu install on my VPS server. Going over the process a second time was a cinch. In case the apps had caused the issue, I decided I could live without them - reinstalling would be no bother, but it's fine, I'll get by. I noticed that the new version came with Redis set up by default, so it could have well been a clash there that was preventing the update from installing, although I think I would have seen other people complaining as my assumption is that most self hosters are likely to be using Redis.

After reinstalling, I also left AJAX as the default for background tasks, as I'm only one user and I stopped using the news app so nothing really needs to sync on a schedule. But it's rare that I log in to my cloud in a browser - which is when AJAX jobs are called (one per page load). My server ended up with a pretty long queue of tasks, so I just set up the Cron job. It's as easy as just editing one file via SSH, restart the Apache2 daemon and NextCloud will detect the change and switch from AJAX to Cron automatically.

I have been keeping my Publii CMS data folder and my Calibre eBook library on my NextCloud, with no issues for either. I have to remember to install my Publii Plugins on new installs, but it's great to have all my stuff in the cloud and also locally on my devices too. I also keep my git projects on there too - not how you might be thinking though. I have my local git projects in my NextCloud as you would on your local machine, so I can resume on the same branch from the same HEAD on any of my machines. Is this wise or foolish? I don't know yet. There's nothing mission critical on there anyway, it's all just my hobbies. The only issue I have experienced is that something in my Vim config keeps creating a file that uses punctuation as the filename, NextCloud (intelligently) doesn't like that and will refuse to sync until you get rid off. If I don't spot it I can log in on my other device and find that the files are not completely up to date, although I have quickly learned to check the system tray icon to make sure everything looks okay before finishing a session at my computer.

Security wise - for a beginner, just forget about it. Sure if you want to learn how to, but if you are a noob, and are concerned about security, just go with a proper provider. I'm not saying it's not possible to have a somewhat secure NextCloud instance as a beginner, but in these times of AI assisted CVE exploits, you're better off leaving it to the professionals.

It has absolutely been an enjoyable learning experience, and while at first there's a lot of new information to process, I haven't felt overwhelmed at any point. I've learned a little bit about LAMP servers along the way, and got something useful out of it. I highly recommend self hosting NextCloud it's the kind of thing that interests you - but again, if you need something done right: let someone else host it. As I mentioned, off the back off this project I have also made a Coolify server at home to experiment with. Although, I have also decided, based off this experience, that I don't think I'd want to host a Got service, as I use GitHub a lot, and I want it to work - and for all my work to be there safely in one piece.

items.title: I Am Learning
items.summary: I've been learning again. Specifically React recently - I did this whole thing once before during the switch from class based to function based components, at a time when the documentation wasn't really keeping up with all the changes that were being made to React. That period appears to be over (for now), and I'm learning React just to get a better feel for Front End Frameworks now that native Web Components appear to be becoming widely available.
items.content_html:
I've been learning again. Specifically React recently - I did this whole thing once before during the switch from class based to function based components, at a time when the documentation wasn't really keeping up with all the changes that were being made to React. That period appears to be over (for now), and I'm learning React just to get a better feel for Front End Frameworks now that native Web Components appear to be becoming widely available.

Whether or not I actually use what I learn as yet to be seen. But if there are native technologies, I prefer to understand them where I can. It might seem a little odd learning React to learn Web Components, and I might be wasting precious time. But I see it as a Front End Framework on rails. I bit like using JQuery as a way to get to grips with the DOM faster than with vanilla JavaScript (that is not how I learned DOM, but an argument could be made for it). React has also become quite ubiquitous and as a result there's a heap of learning resources for it.

I've also been quite busy with my Coolify instance. It's given me the opportunity to set up a WordPress site from scratch. I've only previously edited WordPress website content, and having gone through the set up process, it is astonishingly easy. I can appreciate why it's the best supported and most widely available way to run a full stack website. I might even have a project in mind for it. I'm hoping my tendency for minimalism will keep me out of the infamous plugin hell.

From the collected hours I've spent learning recently, and also not learning, it's become clear to me how much less time I have lately than when I was last here. I'm not entirely sure what's changed. I think it might be my day job getting in the way. But I guess that's just life, and I enjoy my job enough to just put up with it for now. I also need to be able to fund my hobbies and projects, so tit for tat.

items.title: I Have a Coolify Instance
items.summary: I'm like a dog chasing cars at this point. I'm running out of fingers to have in pie's. I started learning PHP a while back, after deciding it might actually be a better skill to have over NodeJS and Python in terms of building a back end. That kind of faded off a bit with other projects popping up here and there. But I had seen Coolify and Dokploy, and had intended on setting one up on a VPS to get myself back onto learning PHP.
items.content_html:
I'm like a dog chasing cars at this point. I'm running out of fingers to have in pie's. I started learning PHP a while back, after deciding it might actually be a better skill to have over NodeJS and Python in terms of building a back end. That kind of faded off a bit with other projects popping up here and there. But I had seen Coolify and Dokploy, and had intended on setting one up on a VPS to get myself back onto learning PHP.

Of course, you can run PHP directly on a LAMP stack, which I'm interested in learning a bit more about too, but having a control centre where I can easily manage lots of different types of applications certainly had high appeal to me.

I almost moved my NextCloud instance over to Hetzner from Hostinger, with the intention of keeping the Hostinger VPS for either a Coolify or Dokploy instance - Hostinger throttles with high traffic while Hetzner charges extra money for it (apparently, maxed out traffic on a Hetzner VPS wouldn't put you too far out of pocket, but I don't really know enough about backend development to feel confident in protecting against things like that). That fell through, as my Hostinger email wouldn't play nice with the Hetzner NextCloud instance, and I couldn't be bothered to work out why so I just kept my cloud on Hostinger.

Having my own Platform As A Service instance still occupied a space in my mind though. I didn't want to pay for a second Hostinger VPS for something that, at least for now, is just experimental. But recently, my setup at home has been moving around. A Raspberry Pi 500+ has replaced my Raspberry Pi 5 as my desktop. That Raspberry Pi 5 has replaced a Raspberry Pi 4 as my smart TV. And now I had a Raspberry Pi 4, with a 256GB M.2. SATA SSD in a tidy Argon One case with nothing to do. It was time.

I researched running a Raspberry Pi based server and how to expose it via a Cloudflare Tunnel, and got to work setting up my own PaaS server at home. This approach only ended up costing me about £10 for a new extension lead and an ethernet cable as I had everything else that I needed already. I'm not sure what it will do to my electricity bills, it's not particularly power hungry, but it's always on so we'll see.

I went with Coolify instead of Dokploy for a few reasons. The main reason being that the Coolify website had installation instructions for Raspberry Pi, so I don't need to concern myself with hardware compatibility. Coolify will run on any Raspberry Pi that can run a 64 bit operating system - so model 3B and onwards. Another reason was that the Dokploy website is heavy. Both Coolify and Dokploy's websites make my Pi 5 chug, and stress the GPU on rendering. Dokploy's is considerably worse, and I was concerned about how the UI would run on my computers browser. Finally, Coolify just seemed that little bit more beginner friendly to me.

Setting it up wasn't difficult. But I did find it to be a little overwhelming at times. Just following the docs get's you through easily enough. But even compared to setting up NextCloud up on an Ubuntu server where it was a completely new experience to me, I still kind of recognised where I was and what I was doing in the terminal for a typical LAMP install, with Coolify however, it felt like everything was new and completely unknown to me. Needless to say I got through it.

So far I've just set up my tunnels, deployed a static website to test deployment, and set up a WordPress website. Once everything was set up correctly, the WordPress website was as simple as just pressing a button. I've had editing priveleges on a WordPress website before, but this was my first time setting one up from scratch, and from a Coolify standpoint, I have to say I am impressed with how simple it was. I'm yet to experience plugin hell .. hopefully soon.

items.title: Bangle 2 JS Apps
items.summary: I finally got around to looking a bit closer at my Bangle 2 JS today. I had some other things on my to do list so I've only loaded a few new clock faces today and looked at some apps. But so far, I'm happy with it.
items.content_html:
I finally got around to looking a bit closer at my Bangle 2 JS today. I had some other things on my to do list so I've only loaded a few new clock faces today and looked at some apps. But so far, I'm happy with it.

I've had the thing nearly a month, and haven't had to charge it since initially charging it. I charged the Bangle and my Watchy in unison to compare them. I really thought the Watchy would win, but that died a few days ago and my Bangle still had about a third of it's battery left - that said, I am only using it for the time and step counting, I've turned the heart rate monitor and Bluetooth off. Still, for doing the same tasks as the Watchy, in terms of battery it would seem as though the Bangle 2 JS was an upgrade for battery life.

I adjusted the flags on Chromium to allow Web Bluetooth and added a few new watch faces. Namely a Pebble style watch face, and the same analogue face I was using on the Watchy (it was my favourite face). I had set up the Watchy to scroll through modes: analogue, digital with date, and a step counter. The Pebble watch face I went with (a non-customisable one) actually shows that's date and steps, so the two birds with one stone (or should I say one pebble?). I looked at a multi watch face that I might be able to use to scroll between the two faces without opening up the settings menu - I had used the same method on the Watchy, using someones multi face code, someone elses analogue face, and a few faces I made myself for the remaining modes. For now I've uninstalled the multi face app as it comes with a load of faces that I didn't really want.

I think next I will explore the Espruino environment and see if I can make the adjustments I want, and explore a bit of the watches inner workings. I'm hoping I can set up a travel mode, that will adjust the time based on a user provided time offset for different timezones, which I had planned to add to my Watchy as a fourth mode before one of it's buttons broke. Watchy will live in a drawer for now, in case something goes wrong with my Bangle, at which point I will try to adjust the firmware so that it can run on the 3 remaining buttons without issue.

items.title: Coding Inertia
items.summary: I'm currently experiencing some inertia with sitting down and my computer and starting to code. It is something I genuinely enjoy doing and like to find time to work on projects when I can. Whether that means spending my day off at my computer or waking up early to get an hour or two in before I start work (I'm an early bird). But lately I've been finding it difficult to actually sit down and get started.
items.content_html:
I'm currently experiencing some inertia with sitting down and my computer and starting to code. It is something I genuinely enjoy doing and like to find time to work on projects when I can. Whether that means spending my day off at my computer or waking up early to get an hour or two in before I start work (I'm an early bird). But lately I've been finding it difficult to actually sit down and get started.

I'm at my computer now (obviously) as I write this. But it's taken a bit of willpower to get here. I tend to guilt myself over not finding time for my hobbies. But when I actually think about it, I've been pretty busy, and considerably tired when I'm not busy. Work had a busy period and I have also being doing lot's of going out things around that.

I spent yesterday avoiding my computer to get some much needed chores done, and even when they were ticked off I kept going to either my TV or my eBook reader. I had decided that the next day would be the safer option. It was raining yesterday, and today the weather is beautiful - it felt like it would be a shame to miss the weather. I took myself for a walk, and had coding on my mind, so I'm back home now. I might take myself out again later for a stroll, or even just go out out if I feel like I've accomplished a good amount at some point throughout the day.

Anyway, I'm here now, and ready. With any luck a blog entry in which I offload my qualms should be all that is required to clear my head and get going. I have a few things I want to try and do, so I'll try work through some of those and see where it goes.

items.title: KDE Plasma Bigscreen on a Raspberry Pi 5
items.summary: The Raspberry Pi 5 does a pretty good job of streaming 1080p video. I had been running KDE Plasma Bigscreen on a Raspberry Pi 4, it worked pretty well, but depending on the streaming service, 1080 video would either stagger or choke. I was quite happy just watching my streams at 720, but with the Pi 5 handling 1080 resolution streaming pretty well under the Raspberry Pi OS, and a new version of Bigscreen in the works for Plasma 6, I thought it was time to upgrade.
items.content_html:
The Raspberry Pi 5 does a pretty good job of streaming 1080p video. I had been running KDE Plasma Bigscreen on a Raspberry Pi 4, it worked pretty well, but depending on the streaming service, 1080 video would either stagger or choke. I was quite happy just watching my streams at 720, but with the Pi 5 handling 1080 resolution streaming pretty well under the Raspberry Pi OS, and a new version of Bigscreen in the works for Plasma 6, I thought it was time to upgrade.

This is exactly the kind of content that goes on my other website, but there's a reason it's here instead, and that reason might disappoint you. I tried a few times to compile the new Bigscreen software with KDE Builder, and when I got stuck, searching for solutions to certain issues often returned the advice "I gave up with Debian and just went back to [Arch/Fedora/OpenSuse]". The guy who originally began the undergoing rejuvenation efforts for Bigscreen got it working on a Pi 5, but with Postmarket OS. It's worth noting at this point, Bigscreen is not available in the Debian 13 Trixie repositories.

For a few reasons, I am too heavily invested in Raspberry Pi's variant of Debian. The first being that it has the best streaming performance of all the operating system's currently available for the Raspberry Pi (at least according to the YouTubers who can be bothered to actually sit and test out each one in sequence). The second being that I use an Argon V3 case with IR remote so I can turn the thing on and off from my couch without having to get up - TV is suppose to be a passive activity.

With everything as it currently is, I see three ways to get Plasma Bigscreen running on a Raspberry Pi 5:

  1. Use an alternative OS (I have already ruled this out for my own use case)
  2. Use Debian 13 Trixie, and add the Bookworm repositories
  3. Use Debian 12 Bookworm

Adding the Bookworm repositories to a Trixie installation is certainly a plausible solution. You would end up with KDE Plasma being installed from the Trixie repo, so Plasma 6, with a 5 Bigscreen package out of the Bookworm repo. Despite some possible QT clash, this should, in theory, work fine. Before I set up my Raspberry Pi 4 Bigscreen installation, I was using a Small Form Factor Dell Optiplex, with an Arch based distribution, and this is exactly the pairing I ended up with, Plasma 6 with Bigscreen 5. It worked fine, and it even fixed a few bugs with opening the settings app's that are specific to the Bigscreen UI. However, I want to watch my TV, not tinker with it. So, for now, I have opted to just use Debian 12 Bookworm, as it leaves me with the exact same set up I've been using, just a little more powerful and therefore able to run 1080.

So, if you would like to set up Plasma Bigscreen on a Raspberry Pi 5, you can follow this guide I have done previously for setting it up on the Raspberry Pi 4. Everything should land the same. Hint: to get the lighter install of KDE Plasma, install the gldriver-test package before enabling SDDM login manager.

sudo apt install kde-plasma-desktop gldriver-test

I would also go straight for firefox after logging in to the KDE Desktop, as Chromium has since switched to Web V3 which has affected UBlock Origin. Firefox ESR may or not be installed along with KDE, in which case it will be IceWeasel (Extended Support Version). Raspberry Pi's mods are for the standard Firefox. The mods package adds UBlock Origin as well as the H264ify extension.

sudo apt purge firefox-esr
sudo apt install firefox rpi-firefox-mods

items.title: BangleJS 2
items.summary: I ordered the BangleJS 2 programmable smart watch. After having issues with my Watchy, and the replacement V3 board suffering from significant clock drift, I decided to just pay out for a different device.
items.content_html:
I ordered the BangleJS 2 programmable smart watch. After having issues with my Watchy, and the replacement V3 board suffering from significant clock drift, I decided to just pay out for a different device.

It arrived the next day, much faster than I was expecting. In between ordering it I had a mere 24 hours to doubt my purchase. I began to wonder if it might have been feasible to instead rewrite the existing Watchy firmware to run on 3 buttons instead of 4, by adjusting some functionality and adding a back option to the settings menu. That may indeed be possible, and I may still try that just for fun.

But the BangleJS 2 arrived, and any doubts I had about my choice were quickly replaced with awe over my shiny new toy. You can't build it and change the case like you can a Watchy, but the trade off is a waterproof case. I haven't had a chance to sit down and reprogram it, but on the surface of it, the process looks to be a good one. It seems a little clunky compared to the typical experience of programming micro controllers, but when you consider that it is a small indie project and the challenge of serial connection to a watertight enclosure, you can begin to understand the novel approach to developing on the board.

Even though I haven't had a chance to tinker with it, I have charged it up and have been wearing it for the better half of a week now. The battery seems good, I've used about 25% according to the battery indicator over 3-4 days. That said, I have disabled the heart rate monitor and am only counting my steps. I haven't had a chance to explore the various sensors or applications, but step counting appears to be accurate, and there has been no clock drift at all since I set the time initially.

items.title: Watchy V3
items.summary: I have read quite a few complaints about the Watchy V3. I try not to listen too much to bad press. A lot of the time it's over the top. I ordered a replacement Watchy from Mouser Electronics. You don't really know what version of the Watchy you're buying in my experience, and just figuring out the correct libraries to use can be a journey in of itself. But after 24 hours of using it, I've noticed one serious problem.
items.content_html:
I have read quite a few complaints about the Watchy V3. I try not to listen too much to bad press. A lot of the time it's over the top. I ordered a replacement Watchy from Mouser Electronics. You don't really know what version of the Watchy you're buying in my experience, and just figuring out the correct libraries to use can be a journey in of itself. But after 24 hours of using it, I've noticed one serious problem.

The V3's ESP32s3 board does not keep time correctly. For a watch, that's undoubtedly not ideal. I'm not exactly experienced enough in micro controllers to figure out why, or to make my own firmware. There is other, apparently better firmware, but I like simple things, I don't want to connect to wifi.

I did also notice that the V3 burns through the battery a lot quicker. My options were:

  • (Easiest) Figure out the time drift and correct it, but this could be inaccurate over time
  • (Harder) Remove a button from the V3 board, and use it to repair my V1 or V2 board, whichever it is, I don't know, I run V1 firmware on it so maybe it's that

The project looks like it may be abandoned by SQFMI. I'm not sure. If they ever release a V4 and it looks as though the V3's issues have been addressed, I'll probably buy it. But for the time being, I decided I will try use a V3 button to replace the broken one on my old board. The old board keeps time impeccably, and the battery lasts for weeks at a time, easily over a month on one charge for my use case.

I haven't done a lot of soldering. I used to repair my electric guitar, which was just soldering wires together, no printed circuit boards there. Soldering the tiny connection points on Watchy's PCB was scary, but I managed it. Unfortunately, you need a pin to pop the button off of the board from underneath, and once that's off, I'm not really sure about how to secure it again. Nonetheless, I tried, and it worked. I had 4 working buttons on my (maybe) V1 again.

But, the solder wasn't enough on it's own to secure to the button well enough. After putting it all back on the case I got about 50 button clicks before the new button broke off. It has only disconnected, and not fully broken like the button that originally begun this roundabout saga. I will try to figure out a way to secure the button, because I liked my Watchy - but I have ordered a Bangle 2 JS. It's not as down and dirty as the Watchy, but the build quality looks promising, and I suppose I can make it as smart, or in my case, dumb as I want it to be.

I'm chalking this one down as a loss, and maybe the most expensive button replacement I will ever do. Annoyingly, I opted for a new board when I ordered the chronologically impaired V3 instead of a replacement button because I was nervous about what might happen if I attempted the repair. And now I have two Watchy boards with 3 buttons each instead of 4. I might make use of what remains of them and maybe make some mini E-Ink displays. A simple web request is built into the firmware, so maybe I could tweak the existing firmware or strip it down to do something interesting. Waste not want not.

items.title: JavaScript Classes
items.summary: I've spent a long time avoiding classes in JavaScript. But I found a legitimate use for them, and now I think I like them.
items.content_html:
I've spent a long time avoiding classes in JavaScript. But I found a legitimate use for them, and now I think I like them.

When I was learning JavaScript, OOP, or Object Oriented Programming, was all the rage. I'm not sure if it still is. I feel like I used to see articles about it every other day, and now I don't. I'm not sure if that's because React switched to function components, or that everyone found a new trend to obsess over, or if I just stopped frequenting the kind of spaces where people talk about it a lot.

I wasn't really a fan. I wasn't against it, I could understand the philosophy and how it might be useful. Like how I feel about React, I didn't feel that I would really be working on projects big enough to benefit from the advantages of OOP. And also, while I was learning, it was difficult to figure out. I'm not sure why, but classes just didn't click for me. It was hard to get my head around it while I was still learning all of JavaScripts traits and querks. And also, I don't think that tidily, my work tends to be messy and is likely a reflection of my mind.

I did however find a legitimate use for classes in a smaller project. I set up an application that needed to define functionality based on data it received from an API. Roughly what data is coming is known, but only roughly. The logic would need to change depending on exactly what data was received.

I had achieved this already with generic JavaScript code and no clear paradigms to hand. But it was messy. It wasn't spaghetti, it was spaghetti soup. And it had been served on a spinning plate. I was having to define an object to contain data then adding data and functions to that object on the fly. It was all over the place.

But then I remembered what classes in JavaScript were. I could define as much as I needed about the data before it arrived, and simply initialise it when I had the data. No errors. Clean. Easy to write. Really easy to write. I was actually surprised how little beyond basic syntax I needed to research now that I've played around with JavaScript long enough to have gained an understanding of scope and this.
